title: North-Bound Distribution of Link-State and Traffic Engineering Information Using BGP
summary: Systems outside a network sometimes need its topology and traffic engineering information, normally carried by IGPs. This standards-track RFC defines a way to carry that link-state information in BGP, so external components such as path computation elements can collect it. It was replaced by RFC 9552.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers know the shape of their own network, because the interior routing protocol keeps a map of every link and router. Tools that sit outside the network, such as a server that works out traffic paths, need that map too. RFC 7752 shows how to carry it outside in BGP, the protocol routers already use to exchange routes.

subtitle: How routers hand their network map to outside tools by carrying link-state data inside BGP.

tldr.problem: Path computation elements and ALTO servers sit outside the network but need its topology and traffic engineering data, which normally stays inside the IGP's link-state database.
tldr.mechanism: A new BGP network layer reachability information format, under address family 16388, describes nodes, links and prefixes, and a new BGP path attribute, number 29, carries their properties.
tldr.outcome: External components can collect the topology using BGP, which many networks already run. This document has been replaced by RFC 9552.

today: RFC 7752 has been obsoleted by RFC 9552, which is the current version of the same mechanism, and it has been updated by RFC 9029. It was a Standards Track document, and it describes the mechanism for publishing a network's link-state and traffic engineering information in BGP so that path computation elements and ALTO servers can collect it.

sections.title: Why and How: Link-State Data in BGP
sections.content:
The contents of a link-state database or of an IGP's traffic engineering database describe only the links and nodes within an IGP area. Some applications, such as end-to-end traffic engineering, would benefit from visibility outside one area or autonomous system in order to make better decisions.

The Path Computation Element is a mechanism for computing end-to-end traffic engineering paths that cross the visibility of more than one database, or that need CPU-intensive or coordinated computations. The ALTO server is an entity that generates an abstracted network topology and provides it to network-aware applications. Both need to gather information about the topologies and capabilities of the network.

This document describes a mechanism by which link-state and traffic engineering information can be collected from networks and shared with external components using BGP. It is achieved with a new BGP network layer reachability information encoding format, it applies to physical and virtual links, and it is subject to policy control. A router's BGP process retrieves the topology from its link-state databases and distributes it to a consumer, either directly or through a peer BGP speaker, typically a dedicated route reflector. A BGP speaker may apply configurable policy to what it distributes: it may distribute the real physical topology, or it may create an abstracted topology in which virtual, aggregated nodes are connected by virtual paths, such as a group of routers in a point of presence.
sections.plainLanguage: The map of the network lives inside the routing protocol, where outside tools cannot see it. This document lets the routers publish that map in BGP, so a tool outside can collect it. What gets published is up to the operator's policy: the real map, or a simplified one.

sections.title: The Link-State NLRI
sections.content:
Each link-state network layer reachability entry describes either a node, a link or a prefix. All non-VPN information is encoded using address family 16388 with subsequent address family identifier 71, and VPN information with 72. Two BGP speakers must use the capabilities advertisement to confirm that both can process such entries, using capability code 1 for multi-protocol BGP with AFI 16388 and SAFI 71, and SAFI 72 for the VPN form.

The entry itself starts with an NLRI type and the total length of the rest of the entry, and the VPN form adds a route distinguisher. There are four NLRI types: 1 for a node, 2 for a link, 3 for an IPv4 topology prefix and 4 for an IPv6 topology prefix. The node form carries a protocol identifier, a 64-bit identifier, and the local node descriptors. The link form adds the remote node descriptors and the link descriptors. The prefix form carries the local node descriptors and the prefix descriptors.

The protocol identifier says where the information came from: 1 for IS-IS level 1, 2 for IS-IS level 2, 3 for OSPFv2, 4 for direct, 5 for static configuration and 6 for OSPFv3. Direct and static configuration should be used when BGP-LS is sourcing local information. The 64-bit identifier identifies the routing universe the entry belongs to, because OSPF and IS-IS may run several instances over the same link; entries from the same routing universe must have the same identifier, and entries with different identifiers must be treated as coming from different routing universes. The value 0 is the well-known identifier for the default layer 3 routing topology.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry says what kind of thing it describes: a router, a link between two routers, or a prefix of addresses. It also says which routing protocol the information came from and which instance of that protocol, so that two independent networks in the same area do not get mixed up.

sections.title: Identifying Nodes, Links and Prefixes
sections.content:
Each node descriptor and link descriptor consists of one or more type, length, value triplets. The length field gives the length of the value in octets, the triplet is not padded to four-octet alignment, and unrecognised types must be preserved and propagated. To make entries with unknown types comparable, all triplets must be ordered in ascending order by type, and triplets of the same type in ascending order of the value, treating the whole value as an opaque hexadecimal string and comparing leftmost octets first. All triplets not specified as mandatory are optional.

Each link is anchored by a pair of router identifiers used by the underlying IGP: a 48-bit ISO System-ID for IS-IS and a 32-bit router ID for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. An IGP may use one or more additional auxiliary router identifiers, mainly for traffic engineering purposes, and these are carried in the descriptor triplets. The descriptors therefore identify the local node, the remote node, and the link between them.
sections.plainLanguage: Every entry is built out of small labelled fields, so a reader that meets a field it does not understand can pass it on unchanged. Nodes are identified by the identifiers their own routing protocol uses, which differ between IS-IS and OSPF.

sections.title: The BGP-LS Attribute
sections.content:
The BGP-LS attribute is an optional, non-transitive BGP attribute that carries link, node and prefix parameters and attributes, such as the link and prefix metric or the auxiliary router identifiers of nodes. It is defined as a set of type, length, value triplets. It should only be included with link-state network layer reachability entries, and must be ignored for all other address families.

The attribute has its own triplets for node attributes, link attributes and prefix attributes, and the link attributes are where the traffic engineering information lives. The memo lists the link attributes a router keeps about its links: local and remote IP addresses, local and remote interface identifiers, link metric and traffic engineering metric, link bandwidth, reservable bandwidth, per class-of-service reservation state, preemption, and shared risk link groups.

The design goal is to keep the dependencies on the protocol the information came from to a minimum and to represent the content in an IGP-neutral way, so that an application learning about a link-state topology does not need to know any OSPF or IS-IS specifics.
sections.plainLanguage: The reachability entries say which routers and links exist. The attribute that travels with them says what each link is like: how fast it is, how much of it can be reserved, and what happens if it fails.

sections.title: Aggregation and Inter-AS Links
sections.content:
The memo explains how a link between two paths in different parts of the network is anchored to a router identifier, giving worked examples for an ISO pseudonode, an OSPF pseudonode, and a migration from OSPFv2 to IS-IS. These examples cover the awkward cases where the topology has to be stitched together across protocols or across the boundary of an area.

There is also a section on turning a link into a path for aggregation, with examples of no aggregation at all, of aggregation between two border routers, and of aggregation across several autonomous systems. The point of aggregation is to let a speaker present a summary of a group of links as a single virtual link, so that the consumer sees a simpler topology.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things make the map awkward in practice: links that cross the edge of an area, and groups of links that are really one thing as far as the outside is concerned. The document gives worked examples for both.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The procedures and protocol extensions in the document do not affect the BGP security model, and the memo points at the security considerations of RFC 4271 and at the analyses in RFC 4272 and RFC 6952.

It does add three points about the peerings this document creates. A BGP speaker must not accept updates from a consumer peer, because a peer could send updates that represent erroneous feedback loops or are simply false input; such protection can be achieved by manual configuration of the consumer peers. An operator should employ a mechanism to protect a BGP speaker against denial-of-service attacks from consumers, the principal attack being an attempt to start multiple sessions either sequentially or simultaneously, which can be addressed by rate limits.

Third, exporting link-state and traffic engineering information may be a risk to the confidentiality of mission-critical or commercially sensitive information about the network. BGP peerings are not automatic and require configuration, so it is the responsibility of the network operator to ensure that only trusted consumers are configured to receive such information.
sections.plainLanguage: The map of the network can be commercially sensitive, so the peerings have to be set up deliberately, one trusted consumer at a time, and the speakers should be protected against being flooded by them.
